Ossifrage
OS-i-frij
noun
From the Latin ossifraga, “the bone-breaker,” from os (“a bone”) and frangere (“to break”); so named from the bird’s manner of bearing bones aloft and letting them fall upon the rocks to shatter them for the marrow.

Biblical Definition

The ossifrage is the bone-breaker — a great bird of prey named in the Latin ossifraga, from its manner of bearing bones aloft and dropping them upon the rocks to shatter them for the marrow. It appears twice in all Scripture, and both times in the same list: among the fowls that Israel might not eat. “These are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls… the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray” (Lev 11:13); and again in Moses’ rehearsal of the law, “these are they of which ye shall not eat: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray” (Deu 14:12). The bird heads the roll of the unclean fowls with the eagle and the ospray — the birds of talon and carrion, that feed upon blood and bone. The purpose of the law is stated plainly: it was given “to make a difference between the unclean and the clean, and between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten” (Lev 11:47). Israel’s table was a daily catechism in separation: a holy people, set apart to a holy God, learned holiness by what they would not touch. The ossifrage was no more sinful than the sparrow — it was a sign. And when the sign had done its work the Lord took it away, letting down the sheet from heaven and answering “I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean” (Act 10:14) with a word that cleansed the meat and opened the door to the Gentiles.

Webster 1828 Definition

The bone-breaker; a great bird of prey that drops bones upon the rocks to break them, named among the unclean fowls of the law.

OSSIFRAGE, the bone-breaker; a large bird of prey of the eagle kind.

From the Latin os, “a bone,” and frangere, “to break.”

So named from bearing bones aloft and dropping them on the rocks for the marrow.

It stands with the eagle and the ospray among the unclean fowls (Lev 11:13).

It occurs but twice in Scripture, both times in the roll of forbidden birds (Deu 14:12).

Key Scripture

Lev 11:13 — "And these are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls; they shall not be eaten, they are an abomination: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray,"

Deu 14:12 — "But these are they of which ye shall not eat: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray,"

Lev 11:47 — "To make a difference between the unclean and the clean, and between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten."

Act 10:14 — "But Peter said, Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean."

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but an old name for a bird of prey; it recovers that the law of clean and unclean taught separation, and that Christ has cleansed the meat.

expand to see more

The word rebukes two errors at once, and they lean opposite ways. The first would keep the shadow: to hold the ossifrage and the ospray still forbidden is to bind the conscience where Christ has loosed it, for the Lord let down the sheet from heaven and said, what God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. The second would despise the shadow: to read Leviticus as arbitrary taboo, a relic of a superstitious people, is to miss that Israel’s table was a daily catechism, teaching a nation to make a difference between the clean and the unclean, and so to learn that their God is holy and they must be a separated people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the ceremonial sign is fulfilled, not forgotten. The dietary law was never about the digestion; it was about the difference. The bone-breaker was no more sinful than the sparrow, but it was set on the wrong side of a line God drew to teach His people what separation means. In Christ the line is not erased but moved inward: the meat is clean and the Gentile is welcome, and what remains is the very substance the sign was shadowing — be ye holy, for I am holy. The Christian’s separation is no longer from the ossifrage but from the world, the flesh, and the devil.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means the bone-breaker, a great bird of prey among the unclean fowls.

Ossifrage — Latin ossifraga, “bone-breaker.”

From os, “a bone,” and frangere, “to break.”

So named from dropping bones upon the rocks to break them for the marrow.

It stands with the eagle and the ospray at the head of the unclean fowls.

It occurs but twice in Scripture, in Lev 11:13 and Deu 14:12.

Usage

"The eagle, the ossifrage, and the ospray head the roll of the birds Israel might not eat."

"The ossifrage was no more sinful than the sparrow — it was a sign, and signs are given to teach."

"The law made a difference between clean and unclean; Christ cleansed the meat and kept the holiness."
